1→# ask-dora skill family

Date: 2026-08-31
Status: ready-for-agent
Source: grill in this repo, 2026-08-31. Glossary: `CONTEXT.md` (ask-dora section).
Issue: [#84](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/84)
Tickets: #85 → then #86 and #87 in parallel → #88 → #89
Related: [Local use-case runner](../local-use-cases/spec.md) and issues #79–#83. This spec does not redo the harness CLI.

10→## Problem Statement

An internal Scalekit teammate opens a coding agent and wants help with Dora.

Today the shipped skill talks only to the Runner. It says: run `dora review --quick`, then fix, until exit 0. That is one job.

The teammate’s real start is a sentence: they type a command and describe an agent they want to run on this machine. Or they ask a normal Dora question (review, fix, unused). There is no one skill that routes both.

The harness already has a grill skill (`grill-routine`) and a routine folder. That grill is not the front door. It does not ask “is this loop-able?” first. It does not check Scalekit connectors. It does not copy skills into the routine. It is not written as a small family.

20→Matt-style idea-to-ship maps do not fit. This product is not “any software idea → ship code.” It is a **routine idea** → a **local** agent that can **loop**.

## Solution

Ship four skills under one add: `npx skills add saif-shines/doraval`.

1. **`ask-dora`** — the only name the human must remember. User-typed router. They type `/ask-dora` plus any Dora question or a routine idea.
2. **`review-with-dora`** — the old Runner loop (review → fix → exit 0). Replaces the skill named `doraval`.
3. **`grilling-for-routine`** — interview for a routine idea. Replaces `grill-routine`.
4. **`writing-for-routine`** — how to write the unattended night prompt. Original text. Same craft as a good agent document (steps, done-when, no second-person). Do not cite or copy another pack.
30→
`discover-connectors` already exists in Scalekit. Point at it. Do not author a second skill with that name.

**Route**

- A Dora job (review, fix, unused, scan) → `review-with-dora` or the matching `dora` verb.
- A **routine idea** (loop, recurring, or an agent that should keep running locally) → the routine flow.

**Routine flow**

40→1. Is it **loop-able**? Can the same prompt run on an interval? If no: say why. Stop. Do not write a routine. Route if it is a normal Dora job.
2. `grilling-for-routine`.
3. Practicality check: live Scalekit connector catalog via `discover-connectors`. Say what exists. Say what an interval job cannot do.
4. `writing-for-routine` writes the night prompt.
5. **Routine copy**: duplicate skill folders into the routine. Source is a name on this machine, a local path, or a GitHub URL. Never edit the original.
6. One live run (print the command, or run it). Missing Hermes: print official install steps. Do not fake a pass.
7. If that run works → **loop** on Hermes. Default interval 1 hour. Dora stays off OAuth. Token fail → `hermes mcp login`.

`dora harness new` starts `ask-dora`, which loads `grilling-for-routine` when the ask is a routine idea.

50→## User Stories

1. As an internal teammate, I want to type `/ask-dora` plus any Dora question, so that I do not have to remember four skill names.
2. As a teammate, I want `/ask-dora` to work when I am not talking about a routine, so that I can still review, fix, or scan.
3. As a teammate, I want `/ask-dora always poll the ooo-holidays channel and create Google Calendar events` to start the routine flow, so that a routine idea has one start.
4. As a teammate, I want the first check to be “is this loop-able?”, so that a webhook or a one-off chat job is not saved as a routine.
5. As a teammate, I want a clear why when an idea is not loop-able, so that I know what to change or which Dora job to run instead.
6. As a teammate, I want no routine folder when the idea is not loop-able, so that disk does not hold a job that cannot loop.
7. As a teammate, I want the grill to ask until the night prompt is specific, so that an unattended pass has enough information.
8. As a teammate, I want the grill to collect skills to run, skills to refer to, and the Scalekit Agent Gateway MCP URL, so that the night pass has a gate.
60→9. As a teammate, I want a default shared MCP URL reused unless I override it, so that I do not paste it every time.
10. As a teammate, I want the agent to look up Scalekit connectors, so that I hear what is possible before the night prompt is written.
11. As a teammate, I want to hear when a needed connector is missing, so that I do not schedule a job that cannot call the tool.
12. As a teammate, I want to hear when an interval job cannot do the idea (push, webhook, human in the loop every tick), so that I do not confuse a loop with a chat app.
13. As a teammate, I want the night prompt written for an agent, so that the loop does not read like a human chat.
14. As a teammate, I want that prompt to use steps and a done-when, so that the night agent can tell finished from not finished.
15. As a teammate, I want no second-person identity in the night prompt, so that the unattended agent is not told “you are.”
16. As a teammate, I want to name a skill, or give a local path, or give a GitHub URL, so that I can bring skills I already have.
17. As a teammate, I want Dora to look up a named skill on this machine first (project `skills/`, then home), so that a short name is enough when the skill is already here.
18. As a teammate, I want Dora to ask for a path or a GitHub URL when the name is missing, so that it does not invent a registry.
70→19. As a teammate, I want those skills copied into the routine, so that later edits do not change the original.
20. As a teammate, I want routine-level edits on the copy only, so that I can tune one job without breaking other jobs.
21. As a teammate, I want one live run before Hermes, so that a bad prompt does not fire every hour.
22. As a teammate, I want the one-pass command printed, so that I can run it in another terminal.
23. As a teammate, I want an offer to run that pass if Hermes is present, so that I do not have to copy the command.
24. As a teammate without Hermes, I want official install steps and no fake pass, so that I am not told it worked.
25. As a teammate, I want the loop to start only after that run works, so that Hermes does not get a failing job.
26. As a teammate, I want the default interval to stay 1 hour, so that I am not forced to pick a schedule first.
27. As a teammate, I want to set the interval after the good run, so that I configure the loop at the moment it becomes real.
28. As a teammate, I want `dora harness boot / pause / resume / list / open` after a routine exists, so that the life of the job has verbs.
80→29. As a teammate, I want Dora off the OAuth / magic-link path, so that a night tick does not wait on a browser.

1→---
name: commit-messages
description: Use when creating git commits, writing commit messages, or when about to run git commit -- enforces structured commit message format with imperative mood, capitalized subjects, 72-char wrapping, and atomic commits
version: 1.0.1
category: Development Workflow
license: MIT
compatibility: opencode
metadata:
  audience: developers
10→  workflow: git
---

# Writing Commit Messages

## Overview

Every commit message follows a consistent format. The subject line completes the sentence: **"If applied, this commit will _\<your subject line\>_"**. When present, the body explains **why**, not what.

## Detect Project Convention First
20→
Follow existing instructions for commits if present in the repository. Check `git log --oneline -20` to see recent patterns and match the existing style.

**Project convention always wins.** The rules below are the default when no convention is detected.

## References

Consider the following references when creating new commit messages:
- **Subject line rules, body format, URLs, issue references**: [references/COMMIT_FORMAT.md](references/COMMIT_FORMAT.md)
- **Split strategies, anti-rationalizations, and refactoring patterns**: [references/ATOMIC_COMMITS.md](references/ATOMIC_COMMITS.md)
30→- **Complete red flags checklist and mistake patterns**: [references/COMMON_MISTAKES.md](references/COMMON_MISTAKES.md)

## Attribution

**Author:** Andrew Fontaine ([@afontaine](https://gitlab.com/afontaine))

This skill is based on widely-accepted git commit message conventions, with inspiration from:

- [Commit Message Guidelines](https://gist.github.com/robertpainsi/b632364184e70900af4ab688decf6f53) by Robert Painsi
- [OpenStack GitCommitMessages](https://wiki.openstack.org/wiki/GitCommitMessages)
40→- [A Note About Git Commit Messages](http://tbaggery.com/2008/04/19/a-note-about-git-commit-messages.html) by Tim Pope
- [How to Write a Git Commit Message](http://chris.beams.io/posts/git-commit/) by Chris Beams

# Writing Commit Messages

## Overview

Every commit message follows a consistent format. The subject line completes the sentence: **"If applied, this commit will _\<your subject line\>_"**. When present, the body explains **why**, not what.

## Detect Project Convention First

Follow existing instructions for commits if present in the repository. Check `git log --oneline -20` to see recent patterns and match the existing style.

**Project convention always wins.** The rules below are the default when no convention is detected.

## References

Consider the following references when creating new commit messages:
- **Subject line rules, body format, URLs, issue references**: [references/COMMIT_FORMAT.md](references/COMMIT_FORMAT.md)
- **Split strategies, anti-rationalizations, and refactoring patterns**: [references/ATOMIC_COMMITS.md](references/ATOMIC_COMMITS.md)
- **Complete red flags checklist and mistake patterns**: [references/COMMON_MISTAKES.md](references/COMMON_MISTAKES.md)

## Attribution

**Author:** Andrew Fontaine ([@afontaine](https://gitlab.com/afontaine))

This skill is based on widely-accepted git commit message conventions, with inspiration from:

- [Commit Message Guidelines](https://gist.github.com/robertpainsi/b632364184e70900af4ab688decf6f53) by Robert Painsi
- [OpenStack GitCommitMessages](https://wiki.openstack.org/wiki/GitCommitMessages)
- [A Note About Git Commit Messages](http://tbaggery.com/2008/04/19/a-note-about-git-commit-messages.html) by Tim Pope
- [How to Write a Git Commit Message](http://chris.beams.io/posts/git-commit/) by Chris Beams

30. As a teammate, I want a dead token to stop and tell me `hermes mcp login`, so that a refresh fail is not a silent success.
31. As a teammate, I want a dead Scalekit connected account to stop and tell me to open the provider link again, so that I can fix the provider side.
32. As a maintainer, I want `ask-dora` to be user-invoked, so that it does not spend description tokens on every turn unless the human types it.
33. As a maintainer, I want `review-with-dora`, `grilling-for-routine`, and `writing-for-routine` to be reachable by `ask-dora`, so that the router can name a real next skill.
34. As a maintainer, I want the skill named `doraval` gone, so that there are not two front doors.
35. As a maintainer, I want `grill-routine` renamed to `grilling-for-routine`, so that there is one interview skill.
36. As a maintainer, I want `dora harness new` to start `ask-dora`, so that the CLI and the slash command share one door.
37. As a maintainer, I want `npx skills add saif-shines/doraval` to install all four skills, so that one add is enough.
38. As a maintainer, I want each of the four to pass `dora review --quick`, so that a draft does not ship.
90→39. As a maintainer, I want original skill text, so that we do not cite or copy another pack in shipped files.
40. As a maintainer, I want MIT on this repo to stay as it is, so that license is not a new debate.
41. As a maintainer, I want README, website, and the family to name the same four skills, so that docs lockstep holds.
42. As a maintainer, I want help text that still talks to the Runner for `dora` verbs, so that Reader and Runner stay split on CLI help.
43. As a first reader, I want wording for an internal teammate, so that this is not sold as a customer product yet.
44. As a later reader, I want objects that are not locked to Scalekit customers only, so that opening up later does not rewrite the folder.
45. As a teammate, I want one machine and one user, so that I do not need a fleet.
46. As a teammate, I want no first sample routine idea forced by this spec, so that the grill stays generic.
47. As a teammate, I want Slack, Discord, Google Calendar, and Webflow to stay connectors on the idea, so that the harness does not assume one app.
48. As a teammate, I want empty `/ask-dora` to print the map, so that I can see Dora jobs and the routine flow.
100→49. As a teammate, I want the map to say when the routine flow applies (routine, loop, recurring, routine idea), so that I do not think every ask becomes a cron job.
50. As a coding agent running `ask-dora`, I want facts (catalog, Hermes present, skill on disk) looked up, so that I do not ask the human for what I can see.
51. As a coding agent, I want decisions left to the human, so that I do not invent a slug, a connector, or a loop interval.
52. As a coding agent writing the night prompt, I want `writing-for-routine` as the single home for that craft, so that the rules are not repeated in `ask-dora`.
53. As a coding agent grilling, I want `grilling-for-routine` as the single home for the interview, so that the router stays a map.
54. As a maintainer, I want this spec to reuse the harness CLI, so that we do not rebuild boot, pause, or the routine folder writer.
55. As a maintainer, I want kit `CONTEXT.md` left alone, so that loop words stay in doraval.
56. As a teammate, I want optional `dora review` on copied skill directories, so that I can check them if I want and skip if I do not.

## Implementation Decisions
110→
- This spec owns the **skill family**. The harness CLI and routine folder contract stay with the local use-case runner spec. Do not re-open those verbs except where a name must change (`grill-routine` → `grilling-for-routine`; start `ask-dora` from `dora harness new`).
- Product words: **routine idea** (typed sentence), **routine** (saved folder), **loop-able** (early check), **loop** (Hermes cron after one good run), **routine copy** (duplicate into the routine).
- Four shipped skills. No skill named `doraval`. No skill named `grill-routine`.
- `ask-dora` is a router only. It does not contain the review loop, the interview, or the night-prompt craft.
- `review-with-dora` holds the current Runner loop. Move that behavior. Then delete the old skill name.
- `grilling-for-routine` and `writing-for-routine` are original. Write them for a local agent that can loop. Do not cite another author or pack in the shipped files. Do not vendor another pack’s text.
- Craft that `writing-for-routine` must teach: steps, completion criteria, no second-person identity, no em dashes, one home per rule, progressive disclosure of reference. Apply that craft to the night prompt, and to the skill files themselves.
- `discover-connectors` is a pointer target only. Do not copy the Scalekit catalog into this repo. Do not ship a second skill with that name.
- Name lookup: project skills, then home skills, then ask for a path or GitHub URL. No public registry in this pass.

Reach for Bun when you need to execute scripts, manage dependencies, run tests, or bundle code for production. Bun is a drop-in replacement for Node.js with integrated package manager, test runner, and bundler.
metadata:

    version: "1.0"

# Bun Skill
10→
## Product Summary

Bun is an all-in-one JavaScript/TypeScript toolkit that replaces Node.js, npm, Jest, and esbuild. It ships as a single binary with four integrated tools: a fast runtime (powered by JavaScriptCore), a package manager, a test runner, and a bundler. Key files: `bunfig.toml` (configuration), `package.json` (dependencies and scripts), `bun.lock` (lockfile). Primary CLI commands: `bun run`, `bun install`, `bun test`, `bun build`. Bun is 4x faster than Node.js at startup and 25x faster than npm at installation. See https://bun.com/docs for complete documentation.

## When to Use

- **Running scripts**: Execute `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, `.jsx` files directly without compilation overhead
- **Managing dependencies**: Install, add, remove, or update npm packages with `bun install` and `bun add`
- **Running tests**: Write Jest-compatible tests with `bun test` for unit, integration, and DOM testing
20→- **Bundling code**: Bundle TypeScript, JSX, CSS, and assets for browsers or servers with `bun build`
- **Building servers**: Create HTTP servers with `Bun.serve()` with built-in routing, WebSocket support, and streaming
- **Monorepo management**: Use workspaces to manage multiple packages in a single repository
- **Replacing Node.js workflows**: Drop-in replacement for existing Node.js projects with minimal changes

## Quick Reference

### Core Commands

| Command | Purpose |
30→|---------|---------|
| `bun run <file>` | Execute a TypeScript/JavaScript file |
| `bun run <script>` | Run a package.json script |
| `bun install` | Install all dependencies from package.json |
| `bun add <pkg>` | Add a package to dependencies |
| `bun add -d <pkg>` | Add a package to devDependencies |
| `bun remove <pkg>` | Remove a package |
| `bun test` | Run all test files matching patterns |
| `bun build <entry>` | Bundle code for production |
| `bunx <pkg>` | Execute a package without installing |
40→
### File Patterns Recognized

- **Scripts**: `*.test.ts`, `*_test.ts`, `*.spec.ts`, `*_spec.ts`
- **Imports**: Direct imports of `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.jsx`, `.json`, `.toml`, `.yaml`, `.html` files
- **Assets**: `.css`, `.svg`, `.png`, and other unrecognized extensions treated as files

### Configuration Files

| File | Purpose |
50→|------|---------|
| `bunfig.toml` | Bun-specific configuration (optional) |
| `package.json` | Dependencies, scripts, workspaces |
| `tsconfig.json` | TypeScript compiler options |
| `bun.lock` | Lockfile (auto-generated, commit to version control) |

### Key Environment Variables

| Variable | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
60→| `BUN_PORT` | Default port for `Bun.serve()` |
| `PORT` | Fallback port if `BUN_PORT` not set |
| `NODE_PORT` | Another fallback port |
| `BUN_INSTALL_GLOBAL_DIR` | Directory for global package installs |

## Decision Guidance

### When to Use `bun run` vs `bun build`

| Scenario | Use |
70→|----------|-----|
| Executing a script during development | `bun run` |
| Running a package.json script | `bun run <script>` |
| Creating a production bundle for browsers | `bun build --target browser` |
| Creating a production bundle for servers | `bun build --target bun` |
| Creating a standalone executable | `bun build --compile` |

### When to Use `bun install` vs `bun add`

| Scenario | Use |
80→|----------|-----|
| Installing all dependencies from package.json | `bun install` |
| Adding a new package to the project | `bun add <pkg>` |
| Adding a dev dependency | `bun add -d <pkg>` |
| Installing globally (system-wide) | `bun add -g <pkg>` |
| Installing from git | `bun add git@github.com:user/repo.git` |

### When to Use `--watch` vs `--hot`

| Scenario | Use |
90→|----------|-----|
| Re-run a script when files change | `bun run --watch <file>` |
| Hot reload with HMR for web development | `bun --hot run <file>` |
| Re-run tests when files change | `bun test --watch` |

## Workflow

### 1. Initialize a Project
```bash
bun init my-app
100→cd my-app
```
Choose a template: Blank, React, or Library. This creates `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, and a starter file.

### 2. Install Dependencies
```bash
bun install
```
Reads `package.json`, downloads packages, and creates `bun.lock`. Runs lifecycle scripts for trusted dependencies only.

110→### 3. Add New Packages
```bash
bun add react
bun add -d @types/react
```
Updates `package.json` and `bun.lock`. Use `-d` for dev dependencies, `--optional` for optional, `--peer` for peer.

### 4. Run Scripts
```bash
bun run dev
120→bun run build
bun run test
```
Executes scripts defined in `package.json`. Bun respects lifecycle hooks (`pre<script>`, `post<script>`).

### 5. Write and Run Tests
```bash
# Create a test file
echo 'import { test, expect } from "bun:test"; test("math", () => expect(2+2).toBe(4));' > math.test.ts

130→# Run tests
bun test
bun test --watch
bun test --coverage
```

### 6. Build for Production
```bash
bun build ./src/index.tsx --outdir ./dist
bun build ./src/index.tsx --outfile ./app --compile
140→```
Bundles code, handles TypeScript/JSX transpilation, tree-shakes dead code, minifies if requested.

### 7. Create an HTTP Server
```typescript
const server = Bun.serve({
  port: 3000,
  routes: {
    "/": () => new Response("Hello"),
    "/api/users/:id": req => new Response(`User ${req.params.id}`),
150→  },
});
console.log(`Server at ${server.url}`);
```
Run with `bun run server.ts`. Supports routing, WebSockets, streaming, and TLS.

## Common Gotchas

- **Lifecycle scripts security**: Bun does not run `postinstall` scripts by default. Add packages to `trustedDependencies` in `package.json` to allow them.
- **Node.js shebang in scripts**: Scripts with `#!/usr/bin/env node` will run with Node.js by default. Use `bun run --bun <script>` to force Bun execution.
160→- **TypeScript errors in Bun global**: Install `@types/bun` and add `"lib": ["ESNext"]` to `tsconfig.json` to fix type errors.
- **Watch mode flag placement**: Put Bun flags immediately after `bun`, not at the end: `bun --watch run dev` ✓, `bun run dev --watch` ✗
- **Lockfile format**: Bun v1.2+ uses text-based `bun.lock` by default. Older projects may have binary `bun.lockb`; migrate with `bun install --save-text-lockfile`.
- **Module resolution**: Bun supports both ESM and CommonJS. Use `"type": "module"` in `package.json` for ESM-first projects.
- **Phantom dependencies**: With `linker: "isolated"` (default for workspaces), packages can only access declared dependencies. Avoid relying on transitive dependencies.

description: >-

  or when grilling a loop-able idea into a routine. Collect skills to run,

# grilling-for-routine

Use this grill with an internal teammate. Turn a routine idea into a routine.
Hermes is the agent. Do not pick a sample product.

## Loop-able

First check: can the same prompt run on an interval?

Loop-able: a poll, a scan, or a check that can repeat with no human on each tick.

Not loop-able: a webhook, a push listener, a one-off, or a job that needs a human every tick.

If not loop-able: say why. Do not write a routine folder. If it is a Dora job, load review-with-dora. Stop.

## Connectors

Load `writing-for-routine` for `prompt.md` and the Fixed-step Skill.

1→---
name: grilling-for-routine
description: >-
  Use when ask-dora routes a routine idea, when running dora harness new,
  or when grilling a loop-able idea into a routine. Collect skills to run,
  skills to refer to, and the Scalekit Agent Gateway MCP URL. After one
  good one-pass, may freeze a deterministic step as a Fixed step.
---

10→# grilling-for-routine

Use this grill with an internal teammate. Turn a routine idea into a routine.
The Runtime ticks the Loop. Today the Runtime is Hermes. Do not pick a sample product.

## Loop-able

First check: can the same prompt run on an interval?

Loop-able: a poll, a scan, or a check that can repeat with no human on each Tick.
20→
Not loop-able: a webhook, a push listener, a one-off, or a job that needs a human every Tick.

If not loop-able: say why. Do not write a routine folder. If it is a Dora job, load review-with-dora. Stop.

## Fixed step

Second preference. Optional. A small loop-able job can ship with `prompt.md` only.

After one good one-pass, freeze a deterministic step into a Skill. A decision step stays in `prompt.md`.
30→
The grill drafts. The human accepts. A Tick never writes. The one-pass does not author files.

Add a new Skill only before the first save. Draft it in a temp folder. The folder writer copies it into the routine.

After save, update only `prompt.md` and the Skill copy. Do not add a new Skill after save.

Refuse Hermes `--script` and `--no-agent` as the freeze path. Those flags cannot call Scalekit MCP tools. A Skill script is local work only.

Load `writing-for-routine` for `prompt.md` and the Fixed-step Skill.
40→
## Connectors

Load `discover-connectors` (Scalekit). Look up the live catalog. Say what exists. Say if a needed connector is missing. Do not vendor that catalog here.

An interval job cannot do a push, a webhook, or a human in the loop every tick. Say so when the idea needs one of those.

## Gate

Collect all three before you write the unattended prompt:
50→
1. Skills to **run** (optional extra SKILL.md folders the night pass loads).
   Say **none** if the MCP tools are enough.
2. Skills to **refer to** (optional folders the prompt may cite).
   Say **none** if none.
3. Scalekit Agent Gateway **MCP URL** (required).
   Slack, GitHub, and other connectors live here. A connector is not a skill.

A default shared MCP URL may already be saved. Reuse it. Ask before you override it for this routine.

60→If no matching skill is on disk, do not invent one. Offer **none**, a local path, or a GitHub URL. Do not treat a missing Slack or GitHub skill as a blocker.

## Routine copy

A skill source is a name, a local path, or a GitHub URL.

Name lookup: project `skills/`, then home skills, then ask for a path or a GitHub URL. Do not invent a registry.

Dora copies each skill folder into the routine. Night-pass edits land on the copy. Do not write the original.

70→Offer `dora review --quick` on each copy. The teammate can skip.

## Order

1. Run the loop-able check.
2. Ask what the routine idea does until the night prompt is specific.
3. Collect the gate. Offer a readable slug. The teammate picks or renames it.
4. Run the connector check.
5. Load `writing-for-routine`. Write `prompt.md`.
6. Print the one-pass command. If Hermes is present, offer to run it. If Hermes is missing, print official install steps. Do not fake a pass. The one-pass does not author files.
80→7. After one good one-pass, offer a Fixed step if a step is deterministic. Draft the Skill in a temp folder. The human accepts. Another one-pass is allowed.
8. Write the routine folder only after that pass, or after the teammate accepts the printed command. Save copies the skills into the routine. Then offer `dora review --quick` on each copy. The teammate can skip.
9. After save, update only `prompt.md` and the Skill copy. Do not add a new Skill.
10. Register Scalekit on Hermes, then login.
   Boot registers it: `dora harness boot <slug>`.
   The same add is `hermes mcp add scalekit --url <mcp-url> --auth oauth` in a real terminal.
   Login without that add fails: server not found.
   After the add, the teammate runs `hermes mcp login scalekit` in a real terminal.
   Done-when: login is the next line only after boot or that add.
   Dora does not run login. Dora does not edit `~/.hermes/config.yaml`.
90→   If a refresh token dies, run that login again. If the Scalekit connected account is dead, open the provider link again.

Do not ask for the loop interval during this grill. Default is 1 hour. Ask after a good run.

```bash
dora harness new --accept --yes --slug <slug> --prompt-file <prompt.md> --mcp-url <url> --skills-run <name|path|url> --skills-refer <name|path|url>
```

MUST NOT let the one-pass author files.
MUST add a new Skill only before the first save, in a temp folder.

  Fixed-step Skill, or when the night prompt needs steps and a done-when.
---

# writing-for-routine

Use this craft with an internal teammate. Write `prompt.md` and, when the grill freezes a step, the Fixed-step Skill. This file is the single home for that craft.

## Shape

Write numbered steps. Each step has a done-when. The night agent can tell finished from not finished.

A done-when is a checkable bound. The agent can see it is true or false.

Write in imperative. Do not assign a second-person identity.

Do not use em dashes.

Keep each rule in one home. Do not repeat the same rule in two files.

Do not name a prompt step Judgment. Judgment is a Dora Finding.

When extra detail is not needed every run, put it in a later file and point at it. Keep this page short.

The prompt is for an unattended pass. It is not a human chat.

## prompt.md

Keep the steps that need a new decision. Name the Fixed-step Skill. Do not repeat the frozen steps.

## Fixed-step Skill

Same craft: steps and a done-when. No second-person identity. No em dashes.

A Skill script lives inside that Skill. Name the helper file in `SKILL.md`. Local work only. The routine has no top-level scripts directory.

## Steps

1. Read the grill answers. Use the gate. Do not invent a slug, a connector, or a skill.
   Done-when: the gate is in the prompt, and no invented name is present.
2. Write `prompt.md` as numbered decision steps. Name any Fixed-step Skill. Do not repeat frozen steps.
   Done-when: every step has a done-when, and frozen steps are not copied here.
3. If the grill froze a step, write that Skill in the temp folder. Optional Skill script inside the Skill.
   Done-when: the Skill has steps, a done-when, and names any helper file.
4. Check both files: no second-person identity, no em dashes, every step has a done-when, no Judgment as a step name.
   Done-when: those checks pass.
5. Hand both files back to `grilling-for-routine` for the one pass.
   Done-when: `grilling-for-routine` has the prompt file and any Skill draft.

```
1. Poll the source named in the gate.
   Done-when: new items since the last tick are listed, or the list is empty.
2. Apply the action named in the gate to each new item.
   Done-when: each item is handled or skipped with a reason.
```

MUST write steps and a done-when.
MUST write `prompt.md` and the Fixed-step Skill when a step is frozen.
MUST keep a Skill script inside the Skill.
MUST NOT add a top-level scripts directory.
MUST NOT assign a second-person identity.
MUST NOT use em dashes.
MUST NOT name a prompt step Judgment.

1→# Contributing to doraval

## Setup

```bash
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run dev -- --help    # run the CLI from source
```

10→Requires Bun ≥ 1.3.0 (see `engines` in `package.json`).

## Before you send a PR

```bash
bun test           # 615+ tests must pass
bun run typecheck  # baseline has pre-existing errors; don't add new ones
```

CI (`.github/workflows/test.yml`) runs `bun test` on Linux, macOS, and Windows. The matrix must be green.
20→
## Code philosophy

Read `AGENTS.md` first. It has the ponytail ladder (YAGNI → reuse → stdlib → installed deps → shortest form → minimum code) this codebase is written against. In short:

- Deletion and reuse beat new surface. Don't add an abstraction for one caller.
- Non-trivial logic gets one small test, not a suite.
- Never skip trust-boundary validation, data-loss error paths, or security handling.

## Commits
30→
Conventional Commits style (`fix:`, `feat:`, `docs:`, `chore:`), matching `git log` and `CHANGELOG.md`. Keep the subject under ~70 chars; explain *why* in the body when it isn't obvious from the diff.

## Version bumps

Don't bump the version in a PR. Releases are cut by maintainers via `bun run bump` / `bun run release` (see `WIP.md` for current release status and policy).

## Filing issues

Prefer `dora report` from inside a project using doraval. It drafts a sanitized issue (no env values, no secrets) with the diagnostic payload maintainers need. Manual issues are fine too.
40→
## Website docs

Canonical user docs live in `apps/website/content/` (MDX). Pick one addressee per page: **Reader** (human: README, install, get-started) or **Runner** (the agent that executes `dora`: skill, per-command `--help`). Do not mix them. Terms match `CONTEXT.md`.

When writing or editing them:

1. Follow the style prompt in `apps/website/.devex-kit/style-prompt-block.md` (or load the `docs-writing-style` skill in review mode).
2. Prefer website MDX over `docs/developer-journey.md`. The journey file is product narrative with a command rename map at the top; it is not shipping user docs.
3. Open every page with 1–3 sentences of prose before the first code fence. Command pages need options, common mistakes, and related links.
50→
## Where things live

| Area | Path |
|---|---|
| CLI commands | `src/cli/commands/` |
| Core logic (review, fix, scaffold, memory) | `src/core/` |
| Provider specs (`dora skill new`, `dora plugin bump`) | `src/providers/` |
| Website / docs | `apps/website/` |
| Docs style prompt | `apps/website/.devex-kit/style-prompt-block.md` |
60→

# Contributing to doraval

## Setup

```bash
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run dev -- --help    # run the CLI from source
```

Requires Bun ≥ 1.3.0 (see `engines` in `package.json`).

## Before you send a PR

```bash
bun test           # 615+ tests must pass
bun run typecheck  # baseline has pre-existing errors; don't add new ones
```

CI (`.github/workflows/test.yml`) runs `bun test` on Linux, macOS, and Windows. The matrix must be green.

## Code philosophy

Read `AGENTS.md` first. It has the ponytail ladder (YAGNI → reuse → stdlib → installed deps → shortest form → minimum code) this codebase is written against. In short:

- Deletion and reuse beat new surface. Don't add an abstraction for one caller.
- Non-trivial logic gets one small test, not a suite.
- Never skip trust-boundary validation, data-loss error paths, or security handling.

## Commits

Conventional Commits style (`fix:`, `feat:`, `docs:`, `chore:`), matching `git log` and `CHANGELOG.md`. Keep the subject under ~70 chars; explain *why* in the body when it isn't obvious from the diff.

## Version bumps

Don't bump the version in a PR. Releases are cut by maintainers via `bun run bump` / `bun run release` (see `WIP.md` for current release status and policy).

## Filing issues

Prefer `dora report` from inside a project using doraval. It drafts a sanitized issue (no env values, no secrets) with the diagnostic payload maintainers need. Manual issues are fine too.

## Website docs

Canonical user docs live in `apps/website/content/` (MDX). Pick one addressee per page: **Reader** (human: README, install, get-started) or **Runner** (the agent that executes `dora`: skill, per-command `--help`). Do not mix them. Terms match `CONTEXT.md`.

When writing or editing them:

1. Follow the style prompt in `apps/website/.devex-kit/style-prompt-block.md` (or load the `docs-writing-style` skill in review mode).
2. Prefer website MDX over `docs/developer-journey.md`. The journey file is product narrative with a command rename map at the top; it is not shipping user docs.
3. Open every page with 1–3 sentences of prose before the first code fence. Command pages need options, common mistakes, and related links.

## Where things live

| Area | Path |
|---|---|
| CLI commands | `src/cli/commands/` |
| Core logic (review, fix, scaffold, memory) | `src/core/` |
| Provider specs (`dora skill new`, `dora plugin bump`) | `src/providers/` |
| Website / docs | `apps/website/` |
| Docs style prompt | `apps/website/.devex-kit/style-prompt-block.md` |

Standards sources:
- AGENTS.md / Agents.md: ponytail ladder (YAGNI → reuse → stdlib → installed deps → shortest form → minimum code). Deletion > addition. Fewest files. No new deps. No version bump unless asked.
- CONTRIBUTING.md: Conventional Commits; bun test must pass; don't add new tsc errors; non-trivial logic gets one small test; don't bump version.
- CONTEXT.md product words: Fixed step, Skill script, Tick, Runtime. Judgment is a Dora Finding. No programmatize as a noun.

Smell baseline (always a judgement call; repo standard overrides):
- Mysterious Name — a function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds. → rename it; if no honest name comes, the design's murky.
- Duplicated Code — the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file in the change. → extract the shared shape, call it from both.
- Feature Envy — a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → move the method onto the data it envies.
- Data Clumps — the same few fields or params keep travelling together (a type wanting to be born). → bundle them into one type, pass that.
- Primitive Obsession — a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
- Repeated Switches — the same switch/if-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
- Shotgun Surgery — one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
- Divergent Change — one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
- Speculative Generality — abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
- Message Chains — long a.b().c().d() navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
- Middle Man — a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
- Refused Bequest — a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

Brief: Report — per file/hunk where relevant — (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) any baseline smell you spot: name it and quote the hunk. Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls — documented-standard breaches can be hard, but baseline smells are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides the baseline. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words.

Return only the Standards report.

- Primitive Obsession — a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
- Repeated Switches — the same switch/if-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
- Shotgun Surgery — one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
- Divergent Change — one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
- Speculative Generality — abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
- Message Chains — long a.b().c().d() navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
- Middle Man — a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
- Refused Bequest — a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

1→# Commit Format Reference

Complete guide to commit message formatting, line wrapping, and conventions.

## Contents
- Subject line rules
- Body format and wrapping
- Long URLs
- Issue references
10→- Conventional Commits compatibility

## Subject Line Rules

| Rule | Example | Violation | Why |
|------|---------|-----------|-----|
| Capitalize first word | `Add CPU arch filter` | `add CPU arch filter` | Sentence case always |
| Imperative mood | `Fix null pointer` | `Fixed null pointer` | Command form: Add/Fix/Remove |
| 72 char max | `Add CPU arch filter support` | `Add CPU architecture filter to scheduler...` | Hard limit |
| No trailing period | `Add user auth` | `Add user auth.` | Subject is title, not sentence |
20→| No scope prefix | `Fix null pointer in auth` | `auth: fix null pointer` | Unless Conventional Commits |
| Meaningful standalone | `Add CPU arch filter support` | `Fix #847` | Readable outside platform |

```bash
# ✅ Correct
Add CPU arch filter scheduler support

# ❌ Wrong
added cpu arch filter scheduler support    # lowercase, past tense
```
30→
## Body Format and Wrapping

### Blank line after subject (critical)

```bash
# ✅ Correct
Add CPU arch filter support

In a mixed environment of x86 and ARM nodes, the scheduler
40→could not distinguish architectures.

# ❌ Wrong (no blank line)
Add CPU arch filter support
In a mixed environment of x86 and ARM nodes...
```

### Wrap at 72 characters

Exception: URLs and code that can't be split.
50→
### Explain WHY, not WHAT

The diff shows what changed; the message explains why:

```bash
# ✅ Correct
Add CPU arch filter support

In a mixed environment of x86 and ARM nodes, the scheduler
60→could not distinguish architectures, causing crashes.

# ❌ Wrong (only describes WHAT)
Add CPU arch filter support

Added arch label to nodes and filter to algorithm.
```

### Describe effects and limitations

70→```bash
Add CPU arch filter support

Enables workloads to be scheduled only on compatible
architectures. Current limitation: only x86 and ARM
supported. New architectures require updating enum.
```

## Long URLs

80→Put URLs on their own line or use reference-style:

```bash
# Option 1: URL on own line
Implement the technique described at:

https://example.com/very/long/url/exceeds/72/chars

# Option 2: Reference-style
Implement the technique at [1] to prevent exhaustion.
90→
[1] https://example.com/very/long/url/exceeds/72/chars
```

## Issue References

**Only add if project uses them** (check `git log --oneline -20`).

Put in **body** on **own line** at end:

100→```bash
# ✅ Correct
Add CPU arch filter support

[explanation]

Fixes #847

# ❌ Wrong (in subject)
Fix #847: Add CPU arch filter
110→```

**Keywords:** `Fixes #N`, `Closes #N`, `Resolves #N` (GitHub/GitLab), `PROJ-123` (Jira)

## Full Example

```
Add CPU arch filter scheduler support

In a mixed environment of x86 and ARM nodes, the scheduler
120→previously could not distinguish between architectures,
leading to binary incompatibility crashes.

Add an arch label to each node and a corresponding filter
in the scheduling algorithm. This enables workloads to be
scheduled only on compatible architectures.

Current limitation: only x86 and ARM are supported. Adding
new architectures requires updating the label enum.

130→Fixes #847
```

## Conventional Commits Compatibility

If project uses Conventional Commits, use this format:

```bash
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

140→feat(scheduler): add CPU arch filter support
fix(auth): handle null session token
chore(deps): update lodash to 4.17.21
```

**Common types:**
- `feat:` - new feature
- `fix:` - bug fix
- `chore:` - maintenance
- `docs:` - documentation
150→- `refactor:` - code change (no fix/feature)
- `test:` - tests
- `perf:` - performance

All other rules still apply (imperative, 72-char limit includes prefix, body explains WHY).

## Gotchas

- **72-char limit includes type prefix** — `feat(scheduler): ` counts toward 72
- **Blank line is critical** — many tools parse on this boundary
160→- **Issue refs in body, not subject** — keeps subject meaningful
- **URLs break wrapping rule** — put on own line
- **Capitalize after colon** — `feat: Add auth` not `feat: add auth` (unless project uses lowercase)

1→---
name: grilling-for-routine
description: >-
  Use when ask-dora routes a routine idea, when running dora harness new,
  or when grilling a loop-able idea into a routine. Collect skills to run,
  skills to refer to, and the Scalekit Agent Gateway MCP URL. After one
  good one-pass, may freeze a deterministic step as a Fixed step.
---

10→# grilling-for-routine

Use this grill with an internal teammate. Turn a routine idea into a routine.
The Runtime ticks the Loop. Today the Runtime is Hermes. Do not pick a sample product.

## Loop-able

First check: can the same prompt run on an interval?

Loop-able: a poll, a scan, or a check that can repeat with no human on each Tick.
20→
Not loop-able: a webhook, a push listener, a one-off, or a job that needs a human every Tick.

If not loop-able: say why. Do not write a routine folder. If it is a Dora job, load review-with-dora. Stop.

## Fixed step

Second preference. Optional. A small loop-able job can ship with `prompt.md` only.

After one good one-pass, offer to freeze a deterministic step into a Skill. A decision step stays in `prompt.md`. The grill may also change `prompt.md` with no new Skill.
30→
The grill drafts. The human accepts. A Tick never writes. The one-pass does not author files.

Add a new Skill only before the first save. Draft it in a temp folder. Pass that temp path as `--skills-run` so the folder writer copies it.

After save, update only `prompt.md` and the Skill copy. Do not add a new Skill after save.

Refuse Hermes `--script` and `--no-agent` as the freeze path. Those flags cannot call Scalekit MCP tools. A Skill script is local work only.

Load `writing-for-routine` for `prompt.md` and the Fixed-step Skill.
40→
## Connectors

Load `discover-connectors` (Scalekit). Look up the live catalog. Say what exists. Say if a needed connector is missing. Do not vendor that catalog here.

An interval job cannot do a push, a webhook, or a human in the loop every tick. Say so when the idea needs one of those.

## Gate

Collect all three before you write the unattended prompt:
50→
1. Skills to **run** (optional extra SKILL.md folders the night pass loads).
   Say **none** if the MCP tools are enough.
2. Skills to **refer to** (optional folders the prompt may cite).
   Say **none** if none.
3. Scalekit Agent Gateway **MCP URL** (required).
   Slack, GitHub, and other connectors live here. A connector is not a skill.

A default shared MCP URL may already be saved. Reuse it. Ask before you override it for this routine.

60→If no matching skill is on disk, do not invent one. Offer **none**, a local path, or a GitHub URL. Do not treat a missing Slack or GitHub skill as a blocker.

## Routine copy

A skill source is a name, a local path, or a GitHub URL.

Name lookup: project `skills/`, then home skills, then ask for a path or a GitHub URL. Do not invent a registry.

Dora copies each skill folder into the routine. Night-pass edits land on the copy. Do not write the original.

70→Offer `dora review --quick` on each copy. The teammate can skip.

## Order

1. Run the loop-able check.
2. Ask what the routine idea does until the night prompt is specific.
3. Collect the gate. Offer a readable slug. The teammate picks or renames it.
4. Run the connector check.
5. Load `writing-for-routine`. Write `prompt.md`.
6. Print the one-pass command. If Hermes is present, offer to run it. If Hermes is missing, print official install steps. Do not fake a pass. The one-pass does not author files.
80→7. After one good one-pass, load `writing-for-routine` again. Update `prompt.md`. Offer a Fixed step if a step is deterministic. Draft that Skill in a temp folder. The human accepts. Another one-pass is allowed.
8. Write the routine folder only after that pass, or after the teammate accepts the printed command. Save copies the skills into the routine. Then offer `dora review --quick` on each copy. The teammate can skip.
9. After save, update only `prompt.md` and the Skill copy. Do not add a new Skill.
10. Register Scalekit on Hermes, then login.
   Boot registers it: `dora harness boot <slug>`.
   The same add is `hermes mcp add scalekit --url <mcp-url> --auth oauth` in a real terminal.
   Login without that add fails: server not found.
   After the add, the teammate runs `hermes mcp login scalekit` in a real terminal.
   Done-when: login is the next line only after boot or that add.
   Dora does not run login. Dora does not edit `~/.hermes/config.yaml`.
90→   If a refresh token dies, run that login again. If the Scalekit connected account is dead, open the provider link again.

Do not ask for the loop interval during this grill. Default is 1 hour. Ask after a good run.

```bash
dora harness new --accept --yes --slug <slug> --prompt-file <prompt.md> --mcp-url <url> --skills-run <name|path|url> --skills-refer <name|path|url>
```

MUST run the loop-able check first.
MUST treat Fixed step as optional and second.
100→MUST freeze only after one good one-pass, and only if the step is deterministic.
MUST draft. MUST wait for human accept. A Tick never writes.
MUST NOT let the one-pass author files.
MUST add a new Skill only before the first save, in a temp folder.
MUST update only `prompt.md` and the Skill copy after save.
MUST NOT use Hermes `--script` or `--no-agent` as the freeze path.
MUST collect the gate before save.
MUST accept none for skills to run and skills to refer.
MUST copy named skills into the routine.
MUST NOT require a skill because a connector exists.
110→MUST NOT write the original skill directory.
MUST NOT invent a registry, a slug, a connector, or a loop interval.
MUST register scalekit with boot or `hermes mcp add` before `hermes mcp login scalekit`.
MUST NOT run or tell login before that add.
MUST NOT edit Hermes config.
MUST NOT write the folder when the idea is not loop-able.
MUST NOT write the folder before the one pass or an accepted printed command.

1→---
name: tdd
description: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
---

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle — consult them before and during the loop, not after.

10→When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification — "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists — and survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams — where tests go

20→A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything — agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"

When the shape of that interface is itself in question — how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose — use the `/codebase-design` skill for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.

## Anti-patterns

- **in-agent → delegate** (Style 1): dora emits a `JUDGE THIS` prompt block; the
  calling model judges inline. Zero keys, zero subprocess.
- **standalone/CI → API** (existing `llm-judge.ts` path). No key → fail clear.
- `eval.judge`: `auto|api|cli` → **`auto|api|delegate`** (drop `cli`).

  CLI fallback to API-or-fail.
- Non-goals: OAuth (parked, ToS-gray), models.dev catalog, prompt-gen (left; still
  protected by the timeout above), in-agent merged verdict.

Grounded in a sourced study of `anomalyco/opencode` @ `67caf894` — its own guidance
for a single-call judge = env-key + AI-SDK `create*` switch + `generateObject`, no
subprocess/plugins/OAuth. dora's API path already is that.

1→# Fixed step + Runtime watch

Date: 2026-09-01
Status: ready-for-agent
Source: grill-with-docs in this repo, 2026-09-01. Glossary: `CONTEXT.md` (Harness).
Issue: [#90](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/90)
Tickets: [#91](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/91) craft · [#92](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/92) watch · [#93](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/93) docs. Order: #91 and #92 in parallel, then #93.
Related: [ask-dora skill family](../ask-dora/spec.md) [#84](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/84). [Local use-case runner](../local-use-cases/spec.md) #79–#83.
This spec does not redo the harness verbs or the routine folder writer.
10→
## Problem Statement

An internal Scalekit teammate has a loop-able routine. Each Tick still asks the Runtime to re-think the whole job in chat.

Some steps are now stable. They are deterministic. The teammate wants those steps frozen in a Skill, with an optional Skill script inside that Skill. The next Tick should follow the Skill instead of inventing the steps again.

`prompt.md` should keep only the steps that need a new decision.

The teammate also cannot see the looping agent. Dora is the front desk. The Runtime (today Hermes) is what ticks in the background. Dora does not print that Runtime’s watch commands where they would help.
20→
## Solution

Keep the loop-able check first. A Fixed step is a second preference.

After one good one-pass, the grill may freeze a deterministic step into a Skill. `writing-for-routine` writes that Skill and writes `prompt.md`. `prompt.md` keeps the steps that need a new decision and names the Skill. A Skill script may live inside the Skill folder. The routine has no top-level scripts directory.

The grill drafts. The human accepts. A Tick never writes files.

Add a new Skill only before the first save. The folder writer does not change. It already copies the Skill tree, including `scripts/`. After save, only update `prompt.md` and the Skill copy.
30→
Dora prints the current Runtime’s watch commands where they help: after `boot`, after `list`, after `pause` / `resume`, and on token or MCP fail. One helper returns those commands. Today it returns Hermes commands. No second Runtime in this pass. No new Dora verb.

## User Stories

1. As an internal teammate, I want the loop-able check to stay first, so that a webhook or a one-off is still not saved as a routine.
2. As a teammate, I want a Fixed step to be optional, so that a small loop-able job can still ship with `prompt.md` only.
3. As a teammate, I want a stable deterministic step frozen in a Skill, so that the next Tick does not re-think that step.
4. As a teammate, I want that Skill stored in the routine folder, so that one job owns its frozen steps.
5. As a teammate, I want an optional helper file inside that Skill, so that local parse or filter work is code, not chat.
40→6. As a teammate, I want `SKILL.md` to name that helper file, so that the Runtime knows which file to run.
7. As a teammate, I do not want a `scripts/` folder next to `prompt.md`, so that the routine object stays prompt plus Skills.
8. As a teammate, I do not want Hermes `--script` / `--no-agent`, so that the Tick can still call Scalekit MCP tools.
9. As a teammate, I want a Skill script to do local work only, so that I do not expect it to use Hermes MCP tokens.
10. As a teammate, I want `prompt.md` to keep the steps that need a new decision, so that I can change those without rewriting the Skill.
11. As a teammate, I want `prompt.md` to name the Fixed-step Skill, so that the Tick loads it.
12. As a teammate, I do not want the same step written in both files, so that each rule has one home.
13. As a teammate, I want a freeze only after one good one-pass, so that a fuzzy grill does not invent a Skill.
14. As a teammate, I want a freeze only when the step is deterministic, so that a decision step stays in `prompt.md`.
15. As a teammate, I want the grill to draft the Skill, so that I do not start from a blank folder.
50→16. As a teammate, I want to accept that draft, so that nothing is saved without my say.
17. As a teammate, I want a Tick to never write files, so that an unattended run cannot invent a Skill.
18. As a teammate, I want the one-pass to stay a test, so that it does not author files on its own.
19. As a teammate, I want the first one-pass to run on `prompt.md`, so that we learn what worked before we freeze.
20. As a teammate, I want the grill to use what that pass taught, so that we add a Skill or we update the prompt.
21. As a teammate, I want another one-pass after an update, so that a change is tested before save or boot.
22. As a teammate, I want a new Fixed-step Skill added only before the first save, so that the existing folder writer can copy it.
23. As a teammate, I want that draft Skill in a temp folder, so that the repo `skills/` folder is not filled with a one-job Skill.
24. As a teammate, I want `writeRoutine` to copy that temp Skill into the routine, so that night edits land on the copy.
25. As a teammate, I want the original Skill left unread-write, so that other jobs do not change.
60→26. As a teammate, I want after-save edits to touch only `prompt.md` and the Skill copy, so that we do not need a second writer.
27. As a teammate, I do not want a new Skill added after save in this pass, so that `routine.yml` is not rewritten by a new verb.
28. As a teammate, I want to bring an existing Skill at the gate, so that a Skill I already have still works.
29. As a teammate, I want empty skill lists to stay valid, so that a prompt-only routine still saves.
30. As a coding agent, I want `writing-for-routine` to write `prompt.md` and the Fixed-step Skill, so that unattended craft has one home.
31. As a coding agent, I want `grilling-for-routine` to run the interview, the one-pass, and the accept, so that the writer is not the interviewer.
32. As a coding agent writing a Fixed-step Skill, I want steps and a done-when, so that the Tick can tell finished from not finished.
33. As a coding agent, I want no second-person identity and no em dashes in those files, so that the night text stays agent-facing.
34. As a coding agent, I want the word Judgment reserved for a Dora Finding, so that I do not name a prompt step Judgment.
35. As a coding agent, I want facts looked up (Hermes present, skill on disk), so that I do not ask the human for what I can see.
70→36. As a teammate, I want Dora to print the Runtime’s watch commands after `boot`, so that I can see the new Loop.
37. As a teammate, I want those commands after `list`, so that I can inspect a job I already have.
38. As a teammate, I want those commands after `pause` and `resume`, so that I can check the new state.
39. As a teammate, I want a required next command on token or MCP fail, so that a dead login is not a silent success.
40. As a teammate, I do not want watch commands after `new` when only a folder was written, so that I am not told to watch a Loop that has not started.
41. As a teammate, I do not want watch commands on `open`, so that opening a folder is not mixed with process watch.
42. As a teammate, I want no new Dora verb for logs, so that Dora stays the front desk and the Runtime stays the watcher.
43. As a teammate, I want today’s printed commands to be Hermes commands, so that they match the agent that is actually ticking.
44. As a later teammate, I want those strings to come from one helper, so that a later Runtime can swap the helper without rewriting every verb.
45. As a later teammate, I do not want a second Runtime in this pass, so that we do not build Claude or Grok loops now.
80→46. As a maintainer, I want `writeRoutine` unchanged, so that the folder contract stays prompt, yaml, and copied Skills.

32. As a coding agent writing a Fixed-step Skill, I want steps and a done-when, so that the Tick can tell finished from not finished.
33. As a coding agent, I want no second-person identity and no em dashes in those files, so that the night text stays agent-facing.
34. As a coding agent, I want the word Judgment reserved for a Dora Finding, so that I do not name a prompt step Judgment.
35. As a coding agent, I want facts looked up (Hermes present, skill on disk), so that I do not ask the human for what I can see.
36. As a teammate, I want Dora to print the Runtime’s watch commands after `boot`, so that I can see the new Loop.
37. As a teammate, I want those commands after `list`, so that I can inspect a job I already have.
38. As a teammate, I want those commands after `pause` and `resume`, so that I can check the new state.
39. As a teammate, I want a required next command on token or MCP fail, so that a dead login is not a silent success.
40. As a teammate, I do not want watch commands after `new` when only a folder was written, so that I am not told to watch a Loop that has not started.
41. As a teammate, I do not want watch commands on `open`, so that opening a folder is not mixed with process watch.
42. As a teammate, I want no new Dora verb for logs, so that Dora stays the front desk and the Runtime stays the watcher.
43. As a teammate, I want today’s printed commands to be Hermes commands, so that they match the agent that is actually ticking.
44. As a later teammate, I want those strings to come from one helper, so that a later Runtime can swap the helper without rewriting every verb.
45. As a later teammate, I do not want a second Runtime in this pass, so that we do not build Claude or Grok loops now.
46. As a maintainer, I want `writeRoutine` unchanged, so that the folder contract stays prompt, yaml, and copied Skills.
47. As a maintainer, I want no new `routine.yml` field for Fixed steps, so that `skills_run` stays the only run list.
48. As a maintainer, I want boot, pause, resume, list, and open left as they are, so that this spec does not rebuild the harness.
49. As a maintainer, I want `dora review --quick` on the two craft skills to stay exit 0, so that a draft does not ship.
50. As a maintainer, I want README, website, and the skills to agree when a help line would otherwise disagree, so that docs lockstep holds.
51. As a maintainer, I want kit `CONTEXT.md` left alone, so that loop words stay in doraval.
52. As a first reader, I want wording for an internal teammate, so that this is not sold as a customer product.
53. As a teammate, I want no first sample routine idea forced by this spec, so that the grill stays generic.
54. As a teammate, I want one machine and one user, so that I do not need a fleet.
55. As a teammate, I want Slack, GitHub, and other apps to stay connectors, so that a Skill script is not treated as the Slack client.
56. As a maintainer, I want this spec to reuse the ask-dora family, so that we do not add a fifth shipped skill name.
57. As a maintainer, I want `#84` left open and unedited, so that the parent family issue stays as it is.
58. As a teammate, I want optional `dora review --quick` on a copied Skill, so that I can check it and skip if I do not want it.
59. As a coding agent, I want the grill to refuse Hermes `--script` as the freeze path, so that a later agent does not reopen that rejected Runtime flag.
60. As a teammate, I want a dead connector at night to stay out of this spec, so that we do not build a Dora notifier here.

## Implementation Decisions

- Loop-able stays the first check. A Fixed step is a second preference. Do not replace the loop-able check.
- Product words: **Fixed step**, **Skill script**, **Tick**, **Runtime**. Do not ship the verb programmatize as a product noun. Do not call a prompt step Judgment.
- A Fixed step is a Skill. A Skill script lives inside that Skill. The routine has no top-level scripts directory.
- Hermes `--script` / `--no-agent` is not the path. Those flags cannot call Scalekit MCP tools. A Skill script is local work only.
- `prompt.md` keeps steps that need a new decision. It names the Fixed-step Skill. It does not repeat the frozen steps.
- Freeze only after one good one-pass, and only if the step is deterministic.
- The grill drafts. The human accepts. A Tick never writes. The one-pass does not author files.
- After the one-pass the grill may change `prompt.md`, and may add or update a Fixed-step Skill. Another one-pass is allowed after that.
- Add a new Skill only before the first save. Draft it in a temp folder. The existing folder writer copies it into the routine. After save, only update `prompt.md` and the Skill copy. No second writer in this pass.
- The folder writer does not change. No new yaml field. `skills_run` is still the list the Runtime loads.
- `writing-for-routine` writes `prompt.md` and the Fixed-step Skill. Same craft: steps, done-when, no second-person, no em dashes, one home per rule.
- `grilling-for-routine` still runs the interview, the gate, the one-pass, and the accept. It loads the writer for both files.
- No fifth shipped skill. `ask-dora` and `review-with-dora` do not gain a new job.
- Runtime watch: one helper. Today it returns Hermes watch commands. Call it after `boot`, `list`, `pause`, and `resume`, and on token or MCP fail (required next command). Do not print it after folder-only `new` or on `open`.
- Do not add a Dora logs verb. Do not rebuild `boot`, `pause`, `resume`, `list`, or `open`.
- No second Runtime in this pass. Do not fork Hermes. Do not install Hermes.
- Docs lockstep when this ships. No version bump unless asked.
- First wording: internal teammate. No forced sample idea. Do not write loop terms into kit `CONTEXT.md`.
- Do not edit or close #84.
- `--workdir` is not decided. If a Skill script cannot be found at implement time, do not invent a folder contract change. Record the miss and stop, or a later ticket may add a Runtime invoke flag. Do not guess that flag in this spec.

## Testing Decisions

A good test checks what a teammate can read on disk or in CLI output. It does not run the interview. It does not call Scalekit. It does not start the Runtime. It does not execute a Skill script.

### Seams

1. **Skill folders (primary).** `dora review --quick` on `grilling-for-routine` and `writing-for-routine`. Exit 0. Assert the grill still names loop-able first. Assert it names Fixed step after one good one-pass, human accept, Tick never writes, add-before-save, update-copy-after-save. Assert the writer names both `prompt.md` and the Fixed-step Skill, steps and done-when, Skill script inside the Skill, no routine-level scripts directory, no Hermes `--script`. Do not automate the chat.
2. **Harness CLI output (watch helper).** After `boot`, `list`, `pause`, and `resume`, output includes the current Runtime’s watch commands. Folder-only `new` and `open` do not. Token or MCP fail still prints the login next command. Prefer the existing harness CLI tests. Assert the helper’s return value for today’s Runtime (Hermes strings). Do not start the gateway.
3. **Docs lockstep.** README, website, and the two craft skills agree when a new help line would otherwise disagree. Extend the existing harness docs test. Do not invent a new catalog page.

`writeRoutine` is not a seam for this spec. Do not add folder-layout tests for a top-level `scripts/` directory.

### Modules under test

- `grilling-for-routine` and `writing-for-routine` (review plus named contracts).
- Runtime watch helper and the harness verbs that print it.
- Docs lockstep test.

### Prior art

- `test/ask-dora.test.ts` (skill-folder contracts).
- `test/harness.test.ts` (verb output, no live Runtime).
- `test/harness-docs.test.ts` (lockstep).

## Out of Scope

- Rebuilding `dora harness` boot, pause, resume, list, or open (TTY pickers, account checks, notifiers).
- Changing the routine folder writer or adding a `routine.yml` field.
- Hermes `--script` / `--no-agent` as the freeze path.
- A second Runtime (Claude, Grok, OpenCode).
- A second writer that adds a Skill after save.
- A Dora logs or dashboard verb.
- A public skill registry.
- A fifth shipped skill name.
- A forced sample routine idea.
- Editing or closing #84.
- Dogfood items that are not Fixed step or Runtime watch: bare `pause` picker, save-time connected-account check, boot-time account verify, a Dora ping when a connector is dead.
- Writing loop terms into kit `CONTEXT.md`.
- Dora on the OAuth path. Dora installing Hermes.
- Live Scalekit or Hermes in CI.
- A version bump unless the user asks.
- Implementing in the spec session. Spec first. Tickets next.

## Further Notes

Glossary lives in doraval `CONTEXT.md` (Harness). Grill closed 2026-09-01.

The Slack + PR approve dogfood was the listen-mode example. Do not copy channel names, mentions, PR URLs, or the Agent Gateway MCP URL into this spec or into shipped files.

`--workdir` and “can the Runtime see a Skill script path” are unknown. Do not block this spec on that. If implement hits it, stop and file a later ticket. Do not guess a Hermes flag.

Next: `/implement` one ticket per fresh chat. Frontier is #91 or #92.

---

- **Standards** — does the code conform to this repo's documented coding standards?
- **Spec** — does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / spec?

## Process

### 1. Pin the fixed point

Whatever the user said is the fixed point — a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc. If they didn't specify one, ask for it.
20→
Capture the diff command once: `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.

Before going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse <fixed-point>`) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here — not inside two parallel sub-agents.

### 2. Identify the spec source

Look for the originating spec, in this order:

1. Issue references in the commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, GitLab `!67`, etc.) — fetch via the workflow in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.
30→2. A path the user passed as an argument.
3. A spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch name or feature.
4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. If they say there isn't one, the **Spec** sub-agent will skip and report "no spec available".

### 3. Identify the standards sources

Anything in the repo that documents how code should be written, such as `CODING_STANDARDS.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

On top of whatever the repo documents, the Standards axis always carries the **smell baseline** below — a fixed set of Fowler code smells (_Refactoring_, ch.3) that applies even when a repo documents nothing. Two rules bind it:

40→- **The repo overrides.** A documented repo standard always wins; where it endorses something the baseline would flag, suppress the smell.
- **Always a judgement call.** Each smell is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation — and, like any standard here, skip anything tooling already enforces.

Each smell reads *what it is* → *how to fix*; match it against the diff:

- **Mysterious Name** — a function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds. → rename it; if no honest name comes, the design's murky.
- **Duplicated Code** — the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file in the change. → extract the shared shape, call it from both.
- **Feature Envy** — a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → move the method onto the data it envies.
- **Data Clumps** — the same few fields or params keep travelling together (a type wanting to be born). → bundle them into one type, pass that.
- **Primitive Obsession** — a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
50→- **Repeated Switches** — the same `switch`/`if`-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
- **Shotgun Surgery** — one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
- **Divergent Change** — one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
- **Speculative Generality** — abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
- **Message Chains** — long `a.b().c().d()` navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
- **Middle Man** — a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
- **Refused Bequest** — a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

### 4. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel

60→**Standards sub-agent prompt** — include:

- The full diff command and commit list.
- The list of standards-source files you found in step 3, **plus the smell baseline from step 3** pasted in full — the sub-agent has no other access to it.
- The brief: "Report — per file/hunk where relevant — (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) any baseline smell you spot: name it and quote the hunk. Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls — documented-standard breaches can be hard, but baseline smells are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides the baseline. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words."

**Spec sub-agent prompt** — include:

- The diff command and commit list.
- The path or fetched contents of the spec.
70→- The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words."

If the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.

### 5. Aggregate

Present the two reports under `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do **not** merge or rerank findings — the two axes are deliberately separate (see _Why two axes_).

End with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue _within each axis_ (if any). Don't pick a single winner across axes — that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent.

80→## Why two axes

A change can pass one axis and fail the other:

- Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → **Standards pass, Spec fail.**
- Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project's conventions → **Spec pass, Standards fail.**

Reporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.
